Pete is a Senior Editor at Tom’s Guide, overseeing the site's reviews team and all cameras coverage. He was previously an editor for Canon’s editorial site, and has been a photographer for a decade. Pete loves getting his hands on and rigorously testing the latest mirrorless cameras. He’s also the Tom’s Guide action cameras expert, putting each action cam thoroughly through its paces.

Nikita tests some of the best cameras at Tom's Guide, putting each camera through rigorous testing by pushing battery life to the limit, analyzing build quality and features to determine whether it's good value for money. She's also the in-house instant cameras expert as she has been using instant cameras since 2015, and drones expert as she’s a licensed drone pilot.

Ashley is a reviews writer here at Tom’s Guide and spends her time testing, well, everything! A lifelong photography enthusiast, she has a keen eye for detail. She's also Tom's Guide's resident ring lights expert — whether it’s golden hour selfies (she considers herself a professional selfie-taker!) or getting the best lighting for pictures of her dog, she is always putting lighting and camera gear through its paces.

Which type of camera do you need? That's important to figure out before you make a purchase. Here's a rundown of the ones that matter (we've included one of each in this guide).

One-line review: The Canon EOS R100 is the cheapest way to get a new mirrorless interchangeable lens camera (ILC), and its excellent image quality and solid AF make it perfect for budding photographers.

People who want to take photography seriously and have lots of creative control over their shots, whether they’re printing them or sharing them on Instagram. It’s ideal for anyone wanting an upgrade from their smartphone without breaking the bank.

The EOS R100 is about as affordable as mirrorless cameras get, yet still offers the essential perks of a “proper” interchangeable lens camera. It has a 24MP APS-C sensor which produces beautiful photos and 4K video. Combined with Canon’s excellent autofocus and the ability to swap lenses when creativity demands, the EOS R100 will give you everything you need to take Instagram-worthy photos.

✅ Beautiful photos: The EOS R100’s 24MP sensor produces beautiful photos with plenty of fine detail. In testing, we loved the natural colors this camera produces, rendering warm skin tones and vivid landscapes — this is Canon all over.

✅ 4K video: The EOS R100 isn’t a video camera, but will still shoot 4K at cinematic 24p, so if you want to dabble in a bit of video, you can!

✅ Great autofocus: Canon’s autofocus systems are legendary. And while the EOS R100 doesn’t have the brand’s very best AF with multiple detection modes (you’ll need the Canon EOS R50 for a taste of that), it still features human face and eye detection, making it great for portraiture and general use.

✅ Plenty of creative flexibility: This is one of the only cameras on the list that’ll let you change lenses (the other is the Pentax KF), which is a big deal. As you grow as a photographer, you can swap lenses to tailor the look and style of your photos.

✅ Solid build: Despite being lightweight and compact, this is a Canon camera, so you can rest assured that it’s built to a high standard and will give you many years of loyal service.

❌ Fixed LCD: The EOS R100 has a fixed LCD, which makes it harder to shoot at odd angles, as you can’t articulate the display to suit. It isn’t a touchscreen either, which means you can’t tap to set focus points.

❌ Limited detection modes: As mentioned above, the EOS R100 only features human AF detection modes, so if you’re after a camera for wildlife photography, we’d recommend something with a more expansive AF system, like the EOS R50.

The EOS R100 isn’t the most feature-packed camera, but packs in a huge amount of functionality and creative flexibility given its budget price tag. If you want a cheap camera to expand your creative horizons and improve your photography, this is the best one to buy.

"Simply put, I chose the EOS R100 as it's great at doing the basics and costs very little. What more do you need on a budget?"

One-line review: The Pentax KF is one of the only new DSLR cameras on the market and is great for budding photographers thanks to its weather sealing, IBIS and great real-world color replication.

This camera is perfect for beginners who want a DSLR to learn the basics on, but which will also grow with them — its IBIS and weather sealing will make it a good camera as you explore more genres and get more creative.

The Pentax KF is the best cheap DSLR because it’s essentially the only entry-level DSLR you can still buy new — making it the cheapest by default. It isn’t the most affordable camera on this list, but its U.S. price (under $600) is very attractive given the feature set. It features weather sealing for shooting in all conditions, IBIS for stabilized handheld shots, and face detection AF to nail portraits every time. It’s difficult to find an interchangeable lens camera with IBIS in this price range.

✅ Strong imaging: The camera has excellent color rendition, strong high ISO performance and did well in our challenging dynamic range testing, too.

✅ IBIS: In testing, we were able to shoot as low as 1/4sec without experiencing any visible shake thanks to the KF’s IBIS, which is rare to find at this price point.

✅ Weather sealing: The camera is weather-sealed, so you can take it out with you on adventures without worrying that it will be damaged if it starts to rain.

✅ Angled LCD screen: The vari-angle LCD screen can flip out and rotate 180º, and is ideal for getting shots at lower angles when using live view.

❌ Heavy: Since this is a DSLR, the camera is much heavier than a mirrorless camera. The KF gets onerous to carry after using it for longer stints.

❌ Autofocus can lag: Although the camera’s autofocus is generally effective, it may occasionally experience lag. This is annoying at times when you want immediate autofocus.

❌ Not one for video: The KF only shoots video at 1080p, so it’s not a great camera for vlogging or video, which is a shame given it has effective IBIS.

The Pentax KF is a great camera for budding photographers and provides great value for money. It takes great images and has an effective IBIS system, the vari-angle display is useful for shooting at different angles, and the weather-sealed body means it can go with you everywhere and not get damaged by the elements. It’s an ideal camera to both learn and grow with.

"It’s the only budget DSLR still being made, but it’s ideal for beginners learning the exposure triangle on a budget."

One line review: The Sony ZV-1F is packed with vlogging-specific features that make content creation easy, and it captures detailed 4K/30P video.

People who are stepping up from smartphone videography, hobbyists, and vloggers looking to take their video content to the next level. It’s ideal for anyone looking to replace their smartphone as their primary vlogging tool while being on a budget.

The Sony ZV-1F is packed with vlogging-specific features, like Product Showcase and Background Defocus, which are usually found on more expensive models. It’s perfect for on-the-fly content creation and to take traveling, thanks to its compact size. It also shoots lovely 4K/30P video, and its straightforward control scheme makes it extremely easy to use.

✅ Compact and portable: Measuring just 4.15 x 2.36 x 1.82 inches and weighing 0.5lbs, the ZV-1F is highly portable as it slips easily into most pockets, and it’s comfortable to hold with either one or both hands.

✅ Easy to use: With its straightforward control scheme and responsive LCD touchscreen, the ZV-1F is extremely easy to use, making the transition from smartphones to cameras seamless.

✅ Lovely video quality: The ZV-1F shoots 4K/30P video and 1080P footage at 5x slow motion by using 120fps. The results are sharp and detailed, and the camera’s autofocus system works well to keep subjects in focus.

✅ Product Showcase: Product Showcase works extremely well for product unboxing videos and reviews as the ZV-1F focuses on the subject closest to the lens while effectively blurring the background. For non-camera-savvy content creators, it makes it easy to create stylized footage.✅ Great built-in mic: The ZV-1F is fitted with a directional three-way capsule mic which captures crisp and clear audio, helping you create content on the fly even if you don’t have an external microphone.

❌ No IBIS: The ZV-1F doesn’t feature in-body image stabilization, which is fairly common in this price range. Instead, you’ll rely on Sony’s SteadyShot technology for capturing smooth and stable footage.

❌ Poor battery life: A single charge yields 360 shots when the monitor is always-on and 540 shots when Auto Monitor off is set to two seconds. This is much lower compared to the ZV-1F’s rivals.

The Sony ZV-1F is a fantastic camera for those stepping up from smartphone videography and looking to take their vlogging content to the next level — all while being on a budget. Its ease of use, compact body, great built-in mic and vlogging-specific features make it the best cheap vlogging camera.

"Easy: it's the cheapest way to get advanced vlogging features and make great-looking video content for social and YouTube."

One-line review: The DJI Osmo Action 4 is a feature-packed professional action camera that's cheaper than ever now that it has been succeeded by a newer model.

People who need a rugged video camera — that means content creators, YouTubers and vloggers, shooting video outdoors, especially if it’s high octane.

The DJI Osmo Action 4 shoots beautiful 4K at up to 120fps, and while YouTube (and most people's monitors) still max out at 4K, you really don’t need more. It’s waterproof down to 59 feet without a case (you’ll only get better than that with its bigger sibling, the DJI Osmo Action 5 Pro) and is built to withstand almost anything the elements can throw at it. It also has a front selfie display for vlogging, and a quick-release magnetic mount for securely attaching and switching between accessories, like selfie sticks.

✅ 4K/120p video: The OA4 shoots beautiful 4K/60p footage, for capturing fast-paced action. If you want slow motion video, it’ll also shoot at up to 120fps in full 4K. It also packs a range of professional features, such as Log recording.

✅ Wireless mic hook up: The OA4 can hook up wirelessly to DJI mics, such as the fantastic DJI Mic 2, giving you professional audio quality with no cables or adapters needed!

✅ An oldie but a goodie: The Osmo Action 4 has now been succeeded by the DJI Osmo Action 5 Pro, driving the OA4’s price down! You can pick it up for just over $200, which is about as cheap as professional-quality action cams come.

✅ So much ruggedness: The OA4 is waterproof to 59 feet, and is fully equipped to withstand the rigors of the environment.

✅ Front vlogging screen: Thanks to its front screen, the OA4 functions well as a vlogging and selfie camera.

❌ No higher than 4K: This camera tops out at 4K. That’ll be plenty enough for most people, but if you’re a pro shooter wanting to oversample 4K, you’ll be out of luck.

❌ Stabilization not the best: The OA4’s stabilization is decent, but not as good as the OA5 Pro or GoPro Hero12 Black. That said, it’s much better than other budget brand cameras at similar price points, like the Akaso Brave 8 Lite.

There's a reason the DJI Osmo Action 4 got the "Best Budget" award on our roundup of the best action cameras. Actually, there are a fair few reasons.

Despite being over a year old, it’s still an outstanding camera for the money, and will record professional-quality 4K video, with great internal audio, easy wireless mic hookup, useful vlogging features and all the ruggedness you could need.

Its stabilization isn’t the best, but it’s fine for most uses, and the lack of +4K recording likely won’t be a problem to anyone in the budget market.

"The DJI Osmo Action 4 is the cheapest way to get professional-looking, well-stabilized 4K/60fps action footage. There might be better action cams out there, but not for the money."

One-line review: Our favorite budget instant camera, the compact Fujifilm Instax mini 41 takes great photos, is incredibly easy to use, and it looks premium too.

Anyone who wants to print photos quickly and easily, without spending too much to begin with (obviously). If you want physical copies of your photos, it's for you. It’s perfect for documenting nights out with friends, weddings, and travels. It’s also quite the bargain given its features.

If you’re looking for lovely and detailed prints with accurate color reproduction, especially in bright conditions, the Instax mini 41 is your port of call. It’s easy to use, and it sports a sleek, premium design. Packing a long battery life as well as a selfie mirror and close-up mode, it’s the perfect cheap instant camera for most photographers.

✅ Easy to use: Sporting a straightforward control scheme that doesn’t feel cluttered, the Instax mini 41 is one of the easiest instant cameras to use. Every button is within easy reach, and each press gives good tactile feedback.

✅ Stunning image quality: Thanks to a maximum aperture of f/12.7 and a shutter speed of 1/2-1/250s, the Instax mini 41 takes lovely photos, especially in bright conditions. Printing and developing is quick at just under 90 seconds, and the photos look colorful and detailed.

✅ Long battery life: The Instax mini 41 utilizes two AA batteries, and the camera can last a total of 100 shots between charges. You can also use rechargeable batteries with it.

✅ Selfie mirror and close-up mode: For people who love taking selfies or like dabbling in macro photography, the Instax mini 41 features a built-in selfie mirror as well as a dedicated close-up mode, both of which work well.

❌ Flash always stays on: Unfortunately, you can’t turn off the Instax mini 41’s flash so it is always on regardless of where or what you’re shooting.

❌ Uses disposable batteries: Disposable batteries can be difficult to recycle so if you’re conscious about harming the planet, this might not be the camera for you.

Cheap and cheerful, the Fujifilm Instax mini 41 is packed full of features at a low price. It's compact and portable, and it looks sleek and premium. It takes fantastic photos in bright conditions, and it lasts very long between charges. Thanks to its ease of use and selfie mirror too, the Instax mini 41 is the best cheap instant camera for your money.

"The Instax mini 41's array of features will suit both casual and serious instant photographers. At this price, it's hard to find such a feature-packed instant camera."

One line review: The Kodak Charmera is a lovely little camera that’s extremely easy to use, and it clips on to your bag or keys, making it highly portable. If space is an issue, look no further.

Anyone who wants a cheap and extremely cheerful camera and isn’t fazed by the subpar image quality should get the Kodak Charmera. As it’s very easy to use thanks to a stripped-back control scheme, it’s perfect for even those who aren’t familiar with the semantics of photography. Oh, and it’s very cute and colorful, reminiscent of 90s tech!

The Kodak Charmera is the smallest camera we’ve tested, and it captures lo-fi images while featuring a straightforward control scheme and menu system. It can record 1080p video at 30fps too, making it a great travel or night-out companion.

✅ Extremely portable: The Kodak Charmera measures just 2.28 x 0.96 x 0.78 inches, and it weighs only 1.05oz, so it’s compact and lightweight. It features a keychain loop so you can hook it on to bags, keys and even jacket zips for easy portability.

✅ Array of filters: There are 11 filters and frames to play with and give your photos a unique look. The four frames feature film-like borders, vintage elements, and even a tiny computer screen.

✅ Lo-fi aesthetic: The photos captured by the Kodak Charmera have a lo-fi aesthetic with plenty of grain, which makes them look like they were taken on an old camera — something very popular on social media right now.

❌ Redundant viewfinder: The Kodak Charmera features a viewfinder but it’s too small and doesn’t display any useful information (unlike EVFs and OVFs on more advanced cameras). It’s less of a viewfinder and more of a hole in the camera.

❌ 1.6MP images only: With a small sensor and only 1.6MP at your disposal, the Kodak Charmera takes decent photos but they won’t win you any pro photography awards.

The Kodak Charmera is an excellent camera for people who want to capture images with a lo-fi aesthetic, and add filters and frames to them. Its ease of use, keychain design, and high portability make it the best cheap small camera.

“The Charmera is cute and lovable, and because it’s so small, there really is no better camera if you want to take one traveling or on a night out.”

One-line review: For the money, they don't come more hardy than the Kodak PIXPRO WPZ2, which impressed us with its competency, image quality and of course, its ruggedness.

The Kodak PIXPRO WPZ2 is perfect for adventurers and travel photographers who like to push their camera to the limit, but it’s also for those who don’t want to spend too much money on one. For $179, you get a rugged waterproof, dustproof and shockproof camera that produces good images and 1080P/30fps video, and it has decent battery life too.

The PIXPRO WPZ2 is waterproof up to 15m/49ft and it’s fully dust-sealed against fine and solid particles. It’s also shockproof and can take a beating, even if it’s dropped from 2m/6ft. This camera is, therefore, great for travel photography as it’s very portable. The PIXPRO WPZ2 is extremely easy to use too.

✅ Ruggedness: For just $179, the PIXPRO WPZ2 is waterproof, dustproof and shockproof, making it the ideal travel companion. It looks like an adventure camera too, with a ruggedly handsome design.

✅ Great photos: Although the camera is limited to taking just 16MP photos, the photos turn out detailed and have a vintage look to them. The camera also has a 4x zoom to aid in all shooting situations.

✅ Good battery life: The camera has a CIPA rating of 200 shots or 70 minutes of 1080P/30fps recording. For a camera of its (small) stature, this is respectable battery life.

✅ Compact & portable: The PIXPRO WPZ2 is also super compact, which combined with its ruggedness literally makes it a 'take anywhere' camera.

❌ Basic feature set: Similar to some other compact cameras, the PIXPRO WPZ2 has a very basic feature set which is limited to 16MP stills and 1080P video.

❌ Subpar low-light performance: The camera adjusts the shutter speed and aperture automatically and its low-light performance isn’t anything to write home about. The camera doesn’t show you how long or short the shutter speed is, which can lead to camera shake.

Overall, the PIXPRO WPZ2 is a fantastic outdoorsy camera that can be used underwater, on hikes in dusty conditions, and it can survive some falls too. Alongside this, the fact that it has good battery life and captures good stills make it the best cheap camera for outdoor adventurers.

"It's handsome and rugged, providing great protection against the elements, while offering the basic photo and video features you'll need at a low price."

One-line review: The Kodak Ultra F9 takes great photos and is incredibly affordable at under $50, making it the ideal starter film camera.

Fans of film photography or for those just getting started in it. Costing just $49, this reusable film camera produces lovely images in bright conditions, it’s extremely easy to use and is very compact and lightweight, making it great to capture holiday snaps on. The Ultra F9 35mm is fit for those looking to populate their social media feed with film photos.

Not only is the Kodak Ultra F9 35mm inexpensive, but so are film and processing costs. For $49, the Ultra F9 35mm is very easy to use as the camera adjusts shutter speed and exposure automatically, and photos turn out great with a retro touch and plenty of detail.

✅ Ease of use: The Ultra F9 35mm is an extremely easy camera to use thanks to the straightforward control scheme. It houses just two buttons so it can be used by anyone, and loading and unloading film is simple too.

✅ Great photos in bright conditions: The Ultra F9 35mm captures lovely images in bright conditions with a retro touch, and you don’t need to worry about adjusting exposure or shutter speed as this is done automatically.

✅ Low film costs: 35mm film is easy to procure and is inexpensive, as one roll (36 exposures) costs just $8 / £11. Processing costs are low as well, and it shouldn’t cost more than $20 / £17 on average.

✅ Lightweight and compact: This is a simple camera, which means it's lightweight, plus it's small enough to fit easily in a pocket.

❌ Can struggle in low light: The Ultra F9 35mm has a fixed f/9 aperture which is designed mainly for brighter conditions. However, it has a built-in flash for dimly lit environments and you can buy more sensitive film for low light.

❌ Tiny viewfinder: The Ultra F9 35mm has a very small viewfinder located right above the film door on the back. Those who wear glasses may struggle to look through it.

Overall, the Kodak Ultra F9 35mm is a fantastic choice for those starting out in film photography. It’s reusable so after the initial spend, you’ll just need to spend money on batteries and film — neither of which cost a lot. It’s easy to use, compact and portable, and it produces charming retro photos, all of which make it the best cheap camera for film lovers.

"This is my favorite cheap film camera because it takes great photos and can be used by practically anyone. It's the perfect way to dabble in film without spending much money."

One-line review: The Camp Snap CS-Pro is a pocket-friendly compact digital camera that we took quite literally everywhere in testing. It takes 16MP pictures that look pretty decent, but the big selling point for this is the lack of screen, keeping you firmly in the moment at all times.

The Camp Snap CS-Pro is the ideal for anyone who wants to capture their adventures. Because of the lack of an LCD screen to preview photos, you won’t be caught up in how your pictures look, and you can simply enjoy the moment. Any fans of the original Camp Snap Screen-Free Camera will love this model too, as the CS-Pro features quality upgrades (including double the sensor resolution) and four new color filter settings.

It can go anywhere with complete ease thanks to its compact size and light weight. Trust me, we tried. In testing, we took it to music concerts, on hiking trails, and out with friends. It held up in every situation and looked good while doing so. It may feel a little plasticky but this keeps the weight down. It takes great photos and demonstrated strong performance in a variety of lighting scenarios during testing, so wherever your travels take you, the camera will be ready.

✅ Color filters: The color filter dial on this camera offers four settings to add a little whimsy to the camera. This means you can even experiment a little with such a simple camera.

✅ Lightweight: At 5.12 ounces, this is one of the lightest digital cameras you can buy, making it ideal for throwing in your bag without being bulky.

✅ Easy to use: It’s a point-and-shoot camera, so there’s not much to it. But the lack of a screen means that you don’t even need to worry about how your shots look in the moment.

✅ Long battery life: It has a rated battery life of 500 shots, but we were able to get even better performance in testing.

❌ Shutter lag: This is vastly improved from the previous model, but there is still a shutter response delay when taking pictures in quick succession, which can prove annoying if you’re trying to get the perfect shot.

❌ Offset viewfinder: The viewfinder of the camera is set slightly to the left of the lens, so if you use this to frame your shots, you need to compensate a little, as your framing will be off.

The Camp Snap CS-Pro is the perfect travel addition for making memories without the distraction of a screen. Its small size and low weight make it a great option for anyone who doesn’t want a camera that takes up a lot of space. It holds up well in most lighting conditions and offers a reliable solution for fun photography with four color settings to choose from. It comes with me everywhere.

"The Camp Snap CS-Pro is the perfect choice for anyone who wants to make memories on a budget. The new model has even had a stylish looks upgrade, double the resolution, and new color filters that make photography so much fun!"

One-line review: A cheap and extremely cheerful point-and-shoot that feels like something from 30 years ago and takes lovely pictures.

Someone who wants to take snaps on holiday and doesn't mind if they can't see them until they plug their SD card into their laptop. This is about as "point and shoot" as it gets — if you want a screen to check things, you'll want something a bit different to this little retro hero.

The Camp Snap 2 is a super portable little camera, and it boils down the act of photography to its most basic parts. It's extremely easy to use — you pop your eye up to the viewfinder, point the camera at your subject, and press the shutter button. Its retro charm is hard to ignore, and the 500 snap battery life is good too. Oh, and it takes really nice images with a nostalgic twinge.

✅ Compact, lightweight design: Measuring only 1.3 x 2.5 x 4.5 inches, the Camp Snap 2 will fit into any pocket you like — and weighing only 3.8 ounces, you won't even know it's there.

✅ Super simple to use: Put your eye to the viewfinder and press the shutter button. This is about as easy to use as it gets.

✅ Good image quality: There's a wonderful retro charm to the images that the Camp Snap 2 takes — and they're bright and colorful to boot.

❌ Plasticky build: This is a cheap retro camera — don't expect sumptuous materials or premium build quality.

❌ Laggy shutter: Pressing the shutter button doesn't immediately activate the shutter. There's a slightly irritating delay.

This is a cheap, cheap camera that's packed full of fun features. The lack of a screen might seem like a problem, but it really reconnects you with the act of taking a photo — and the images themselves are great too. Why is it the best point-and-shoot camera? Because it does two things, and it does them both very well. It points, and it shoots.

"I love the Camp Snap 2 and its retro styling — the fun nostalgic filters are loads of fun too."

One-line review: Despite its tiny stature and budget price, the DJI Neo is absolutely stuffed to the brim with features and doesn't require FAA registration.

The DJI Neo is for drone novices or enthusiasts on a budget who are looking to enter the world of drone photography. For the features it offers, this drone is excellent value for money.

The Neo is great for those starting out in drone photography because everything is done automatically — from exposure to ISO. It’s extremely easy to fly either with your smartphone or the RC-N3 controller, and its small size makes it the perfect travel companion. The Neo is capable of shooting 4K video at 30fps and capturing 12MP stills. It has been succeeded by the DJI Neo 2, but that drone is quite a bit pricier, so we still favor the original Neo for this guide.

✅ Easy to fly: You can control the Neo either via the DJI Fly app on a smartphone or the RC-N3 controller, and both ways are straightforward. The RC-N3 comes with two detachable joysticks which are highly responsive and comfortable to use for long hours.

✅ User-friendly app: DJI's app is free to download and easy to use, while also providing lots of functionality and control.

✅ Compact and lightweight: The Neo weighs just 4.76 ounces which means you don’t need to obtain a license to fly it (but it’s still worth checking local laws before flying). This also means it’s very easy to travel with.

✅ Smooth 4K footage: The Neo shoots 4K video at 30fps or 1080P at 60fps, which is great for the price. Footage is smooth with plenty of detail, as is panning across a scene. Its f/2.8 aperture also delivers good results in moderately lit conditions.

✅ Very affordable: At under $200, this is one of the cheapest and best drones you can buy.

❌ Short flight time: On a single charge, the Neo has a flight time of just 18 minutes which is about half the time you get with DJI’s other drones. It’s worth investing in the Fly More combo which gives you two spare batteries to bump the total flying time up to 54 minutes.

❌ No obstacle avoidance: Unlike pricier DJI drones, the Neo doesn’t feature smart obstacle avoidance. This means that the drone can’t automatically dodge walls or trees, so you’ll have to be mindful of its position in the air at all times.

The Neo is a beginner-friendly drone that doesn’t cost a fortune, making it the ideal choice for aerial enthusiasts. The ability to capture gorgeous 4K footage and detailed stills, combined with its ease of use and lightweight body, makes the Neo the best cheap drone camera.

"The DJI Neo may not be the latest DJI beginner drone, but it still boasts fantastic specs and features for beginner pilots, all at a price that can't be beat."

Panasonic Lumix G97 ★★★★Considered for: Best cheap mirrorless cameraThe Lumix G97 is a great little camera, that produces solid images, offers decent handling and even boasts a form of IBIS (but only when paired with an OIS lens). Its AF is out of date for a modern camera, though, so we prefer the Canon EOS R100 for our best cheap mirrorless award.

Potensic Atom 2 ★★★★½Considered for: Best cheap droneThe Potensic Atom 2 is the closest competitor to the DJI Neo in the cheap, entry-level drones category. We loved its 4K video, 48MP stills, AI subject tracking and intuitive controller. At the end of the day though, the DJI Neo, which is also an epic drone, won for one simple reason: it's cheaper.

Pentax WG-1000 ★★★★Considered for: Best cheap rugged cameraWe liked the Pentax WG-1000 during testing. It shot decent stills and was indeed rugged. However, it's more expensive than the Kodak PIXPRO WPZ2 but doesn't offer much more.

Fujifilm Instax mini 12 ★★★★Considered for: Best cheap instant cameraAh, the legendary Instax mini 12. Make no mistake, we love this camera, and it holds the best for beginners award on our roundup of the best instant cameras. However, the Polaroid Go Gen 2 (holds the top spot on our instant cams roundup) offers a lot more for very little extra cash.

When buying a cheap camera, you’re naturally going to have to sacrifice a few things. The latest and greatest cameras simply don’t come cheap. Usually, you’ll either have to accept an older model, or sacrifice features.

However, you absolutely don’t have to sacrifice quality. You can pick up some great cameras for well under $100, and they aren’t just cheap crap. And that’s where we come in! This guide is designed to help you filter out the cameras that are cheap, yet still great quality and built to last.

The specific features you need to look for will depend on what you’re using the camera for. If you want to take really nice photos and grow as a photographer, then you’ll want a camera with a larger sensor, decent megapixel count and good autofocus — that means you’ll need to splash out on a DSLR or mirrorless camera.

Shooting video? You’ll want 4K footage, decent stabilization and the ability to connect external microphones. A vlogging camera is ideal, or an action camera if you’ll be shooting outdoors or in extreme environments. If you’re after sky-high footage, then you’ll want a drone (and yes, you can absolutely pick up great drones without breaking the bank).

Want to print your photos? You have a few options. The high-resolution sensors in mirrorless cameras will yield the best results when printing digital images. If you want the film look, you can go for an instant camera, which will be best for immediate printing and documenting social events, or a film camera, which will produce higher quality prints but requires film to be developed.

If you need a camera for travel, then it’s all about portability. You’ll want something that takes decent photos, but is small enough to fit in a pocket or backpack, and which won’t become a chore when worn around your neck.

Every single camera on this list has been through the Tom’s Guide reviews process, which means they’ve all been thoroughly tested by Tom’s Guide experts. The testing process naturally differs for the different categories of cameras — we test an action camera differently to how we test an instant camera, for example.

However, there are many things all cameras have in common. We always test how sharp the camera optics are, looking for optical distortions and image artefacts. We always evaluate how well images turn out, how detailed they are and the color accuracy of the camera. We take lots of test shots or videos with each camera, enabling us to test autofocus, exposure metering and all the extra features such as AF modes.

Naturally, we always evaluate the price of a product, test its build quality, and analyze both how easy the camera is to use and how sensibly it’s laid out. If there’s a smartphone app, we use it and evaluate how many extra features it adds, but also how user-friendly it is. We always evaluate the battery life of cameras, too.

We don’t just list the specs or features of these cameras either, and always analyze whether each of a camera’s features is good or bad, and why — that involves weighing it up against the product’s cost and competition. Throughout each review, we constantly compare each product to its rivals to help you make the most informed purchase. We’ve included links to the individual reviews for each camera within every entry, so you can get the full lowdown on each product if you want to know more.

Why spend money on even a cheap camera when you have your smartphone, right? Won't your phone take pictures just as well?

That depends on the phone and indeed the camera, but generally speaking a decent dedicated camera will be able to take better photos than your smartphone. Phones have small image sensors, as there isn't much space inside a phone case for a large sensor. The iPhone 16 uses a 1/1.29-inch sensor, which is a lot smaller than the APS-C sensor used in the Canon EOS R100. A larger sensor delivers cleaner images in low light. That said, many phones these days feature larger sensors than some cameras, especially compact cameras.

Another factor is optics. Smartphones have to use small lenses — again, as space is a major consideration. Smaller lenses just can't match the sharpness and quality of larger lenses on dedicated cameras, especially those on interchangeable lens cameras (like mirrorless or DSLR bodies).

And while some smartphones offer manual controls, often these aren't truly manual. You can adjust "aperture" on an iPhone, for instance, but the phone simply applies a software-generated blur to approximate the look of a shallow depth of field at wide apertures. While this looks OK at a glance, study the image closely and you'll see mistakes and things blurred that shouldn't be. This reliance on software is repeated in other areas by your smartphone camera, and generally results in poorer image quality.

And finally, there's use case. If you want to shoot film photos, or print your photos instantly, you can't do either with a smartphone alone. Using a dedicated camera is often more fun, too! There's something special about the experience of using a camera that smartphones can't quite replicate.

That really depends on the category of camera you need, and the definition of “cheap” changes based on said category. If you want the best image quality or a vlogging camera, you’ll need a mirrorless camera like the EOS R100, and cheap means around the $250-$400 mark. Action cameras, expect to spend around $175 - $200 for a cheap model.

Great instant cameras and compact cameras can easily be found for around the $100 mark, while affordable film cameras can be yours for very little more. If you want a cheap drone, you can expect to spend in the vicinity of $200.

No. Or at least, not until they're sure they want to get into photography. Cheap cameras are a great way to see if you like photography (or shooting video), and whether you really want to put in the time and dedication to learn and gain experience.

That's not to say you should buy the cheapest camera you can find, though, as there are many terrible cameras out there which are a total waste of money. You should buy a decent camera which will allow you to learn without breaking the bank. And that's where this guide comes in! It will help you choose a cheap camera that's also good quality.

#3203. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.)

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue

Tereza Pultarova is a London-based journalist specializing in aerospace and defense technologies. She is a native of the Czech Republic.

I enjoyed this piece very, very much, and I truly hope this team continues its work.

Those are some pretty impressive photos! It also seems like the iron ion filtering is pretty unique. I love seeing cases where people build something they want to see in the world with minimal outside support. Seems like it would be a solid return on more public money to seek out and support scrappy projects like this one.

#3202. These Are the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Kindles and E-Readers

Amazon's Black Friday sale kicked off today, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers. Timing your purchase is now a bigger deal than ever (so to speak), as Amazon recently raised the price of basically every Kindle by $50 or more due to the ongoing RAM crisis.

Because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save big on a few worthy Kindle alternatives. Here are your e-reader best bets in the lead-up to Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people. An upgraded version of the basic Kindle, the Paperwhite adds a larger screen, temperature-adjustable lighting, water resistance, and better battery life—and if you opt for the Signature Edition, you also get double the storage and no lock screen ads. Earlier this year, it jumped in price to $250, even before the company introduced a new model—but you can get the 2024 model for $179.99, 28% off the new list price.

If you want a great Kindle but you don't care about paying extra for more storage or getting rid of lock screen ads, the non-Signature Edition of the Kindle Paperwhite is also a great buy right now. The 2024 model has been discounted to $129.99 from the list price of $199.99. It's available in standard black, Jade, or Raspberry colors.

If you don't need the bells and whistles of the Paperwhite, you can also pick up the standard Kindle. It's still a very capable device, with good lighting, 16GB of onboard storage, and the ability to hook up your Bluetooth speakers to listen to Audible audiobooks. The standard Kindle, which now retails for $150, is marked down to $119.99, making it the cheapest Kindle option. Though I think it makes more sense to spend $10 more on the Signature Edition, this is the way to go if you want the cute Matcha color.

If you like to read comics or you just appreciate looking at your book covers in full color, the 2024 Kindle Colorsoft is also at a strong 41% discount for Black Friday, bringing it down to around $170. For $10 less than the Paperwhite Signature edition, you get all the same perks (including an ad-free experience) and a color e-ink screen that's great for reading magazines, graphic novels, and manga. Color e-ink isn't for everyone, but if it's for you, the Colorsoft has the best color screen on the market. For an extra $10, the Colorsoft Kids Edition adds a case, a yearlong subscription to Kindle Kids+, and an extended warranty.

If you're looking for a combination e-reader and e-notebook, the Kindle Scribe is a great option. With a larger screen than Amazon's other e-readers, it offers all the benefits of the Paperwhite but adds support for the excellent Premium Pen stylus, allowing you to take notes in your Amazon e-books or create handwritten documents that you can later convert to text using the onboard AI tools. The 32GB black-and-white version of the Kindle Scribe is currently $349.99, while the Colorsoft version will run you $449.99. Both of these are the newest models, released in 2025.

The new Kindle Scribe Colorsoft has all the same great features of the black-and-white version discussed above, but adds a full-color e-ink display. Combined with the large 11-inch screen, this makes it a great device for reading comics or magazine articles as they were meant to be read, or marking up PDFs using the included Premium Pen. This device usually costs a hefty $630, but the current Black Friday sale cuts $180 off of that price.

If you want to step outside of the Amazon ecosystem, the Kobo Libra Colour is a good bet. Discounted $30 to $229.99 at Best Buy, it's currently pricier than the Kindle Colorsoft, but you get a bit more for your money. While most of the specs are similar (they both use the same Kaleido 3 screen and offer 32GB of storage), the Kobo supports a stylus, so you can jot down notes in your books or keep a digital journal. It also has physical page-turn buttons, which the Colorsoft lacks.

If you don't want to be tied to the Amazon ecosystem and/or you're looking for a device that's a bit more portable, consider the Viwoods AiPaper Reader, currently marked down to $200, its lowest price ever. It's got a 6.13-inch screen, so it's the same size and shape as your phone, and it has a crisp e-ink screen with a strong (if not temperature-adjustable) front light and 128GB of onboard storage. The best part is, it runs on an open Android system, so you can install multiple reading apps, including Kindle, Nook, Kobo, and Libby, and keep all of your books in one place. (Check out my review of the Viwoods AiPaper Reader for more—it's a nifty little device.)

If you don't have a large Kindle library, you're moderately tech-savvy, and you praise portability above all else, I can't recommend Xteink's line of e-readers more highly. The 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic is at its lowest price ever, coming in at just under $55, around $34 off the list price. Meanwhile, the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 is about a dollar more; that's a less-generous 19% discount. I own both, and while the Classic is definitely worth the current sale price, I actually prefer the form factor of the smaller X3 (currently $55.72), which is about the size of a library card.

For about $30 more than the X4 Classic, you can upgrade to the Xteink X4 Pro, which happens to be Lifehacker's e-reader Gift of the Year pick. It offers all the perks of the other Xteink devices, with two critical quality-of-life upgrades: A touchscreen for easier navigation, and a temperature-adjustable front light so you can read it in a dark room. (Less obviously, it also has a slightly faster processor that makes the whole thing feel a little snappier.) Right now, the X4 Pro is at its lowest price ever when ordered directly from Xteink: $84, or around 15% off the usual $99 price.

If you're feeling tentative about trusting a seemingly no-name Chinese tech brand, read more about the devices in my review, or listen to the collected wisdom of the tens of thousands of people in the bustling r/xteink Reddit group.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.
